newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Thousands flock to Bethlehem but joy muted.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flock to Bethlehem but joy muted.

text.p: Tens of thousands of pilgrims flocked on Christmas Eve to the Palestinian town where Jesus was born, but residents could still only dream of a joyous holiday in a region still plagued by conflict.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, buoyed by progress towards a self-rule deal on Hebron, went straight to Bethlehem in the West Bank from a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Gaza.
Israel even took some of the shine off festivities in Bethlehem this year, preventing a Finnish Christmas tree from reaching the town for fear of what officials said was the spread of disease.

Arafat's Christian-born wife Suha lit a modest local tree to launch official Christmas celebrations on Monday. On Tuesday, a large crowd headed by the Palestinian first lady and Latin Patriarch Michel Sabbah thronged the city.
Celebrations reflected changes brought about by Israel's pullout from the town of 40,000 Moslem and Christian Arabs four days before Christmas last year.

Bands of revelers and carolers meandered through Manger Square while a hazy moon hung low over the Church of Nativity. Loudspeakers blared classical Arabic music and Christmas songs with a disco beat.

"It's a very beautiful scene today. This is the most well-organised Christmas in 20 years and even more organised than last year's," Anton Antonia, who manages the Christmas Tree Resturant on Manger Square.
He said the more than 30,000 tourists in the town represented a 50 percent increase over last year.
But more than three years after Israel and the PLO signed a landmark peace accord, Bethlehem's Palestinians complain that over all they have yet to see the dividends of peace.

Although they sit on a treasure trove of historic sites that millions of Christians around the world dream of visiting, many businessmen in Bethlehem say dreams of prosperity after peace have yet to be fulfilled.

Despite the Christmas rush George Sammour, director of Tourism Industries and Licensing at the Palestinian Tourism Ministry, said about 960,000 tourists had visited Bethlehem this year, down 12 percent from last year.

"The celebration is very nice but it is not reflected in business. We don't have business at all because of the closure and the political and security situation," Salim Hawareen, manager of al-Andalus Hotel on Manger Square, told Reuters.
An unfinished peace accord, political instability and violence continue to stifle tourism for both Israelis and Palestinians.

Israeli clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza because of suicide attacks that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March. Israel's opening of a tourist tunnel near Islamic sites in Jerusalem ignited violence in September that claimed the lives of 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis.
"The closure is really killing us. It is killing our business and killing us. But I am very happy today because of the celebrations," Hawareen said.
For many pilgrims, the experience was unforgettable.
"It's a wonderful experience to be in Bethlehem...If you experience Bethlehem there is no other experience to talk about," said Mary Jane Lally, a Canadian tourist who arrived with her three sons.
The Lallys did not fear Israeli-Palestinian clashes, she said. "We thought about this, but we decided to come...We didn't have any thoughts that this would happen again."
